Learning Objectives
Describe risk factors associated with venous thromboembolism.
Recognize the diagnostic findings of venous thromboembolism.

Patients undergoing orthopaedic procedures have a higher risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
or pulmonary embolism than patients undergoing other surgical procedures.
Patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty have an even higher risk of venous
thromboembolism (VTE) than patients undergoing other orthopaedic procedures.
All patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty should receive VTE prophylaxis.
VTE prophylaxis should be tailored based on risk stratification.

Overview
In patients undergoing orthopaedic procedures, the risk of postoperative VTE (DVT and
pulmonary embolism) is among the highest for all surgical specialties.1 VTE is a notable
reason for morbidity and a cause for increased hospital costs postoperatively.
Appropriate prophylaxis may reduce mortality.2 All patients undergoing total joint
arthroplasty (TJA) are at risk for VTE because of surgery-related factors, including
tourniquet use causing venous blood stasis, manipulations of the limb causing
endothelial vascular injuries, and use of polymethyl methacrylate bone cement
increasing hypercoagulability. In addition, these patients may have reduced mobility
preoperatively and postoperatively.3-5 Therefore, in patients undergoing TJA,
prophylactic measures must be taken to reduce the risk of VTE.6,7
Epidemiology
The 90-day incidence of VTE is variable and may be as high as 5% for DVT and as high as 2% for
pulmonary embolism in patients receiving prophylaxis.
The 10-year incidence of recurrent VTE may be as high as 39.9% (range, 35.4% to 44.4%).
Death within 1 month of diagnosis occurs in approximately 6% of patients with DVT and
approximately 12% of patients with pulmonary embolism.

Epidemiology

In the United States, more than 540,000 total knee arthroplasty procedures and more
than 230,000 total hip arthroplasty procedures are performed annually, and this rate is
constantly increasing.8 Patients who undergo such procedures are considered a high-
risk group for VTE compared with patients undergoing other surgical procedures.6 Exact
assessments of the baseline VTE risk in the absence of prophylaxis have been hindered
by factors including the derivation of data from heterogeneous populations, the
reporting of symptomatic and asymptomatic events, and the reduced prevalence of VTE
likely because of the increasing use of thromboprophylaxis and early ambulation during
hospital stays. Without pharmacologic prophylaxis, asymptomatic DVT (detected via
routine contrast venography) was present in 54% and 64% of patients who underwent
total hip arthroplasty and total knee arthroplasty, and 27% and 15% of these were
proximal thrombosis, respectively.9 However, rates of symptomatic VTE are far lower
and range from 2% to 3% without pharmacologic prophylaxis and from 1% to 1.2% (1:3
in favor of DVT compared with pulmonary embolism) with pharmacologic prophylaxis.
VTE is a common cause of readmission and increased hospital costs, which double for
patients in whom VTE occurs postoperatively.10 VTE also is linked to possible future
complications, including postthrombotic syndrome, cardiopulmonary sequelae,
recurrence, major bleeding associated with anticoagulation, and other adverse events.
Etiology
The Virchow triad consists of venous stasis, endothelial damage, and hypercoagulation.
All three factors are closely related to hip and knee arthroplasty.
The clotting mechanism consists of an intrinsic and an extrinsic pathway; both pathways are
found at the level of factor X, transformed into factor Xa.

Etiology
More than 150 years ago, Rudolf Virchow defined the triad of factors accountable for
thrombosis: venous stasis, endothelial damage, and hypercoagulation. All three factors
are closely linked to knee and hip arthroplasty. Thrombosis formation begins during TJA
because a major reduction in venous drainage occurs. Local areas of stasis as a result of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:01 AM
AAOS | Venous Thromboembolism in Knee and Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000020
3/19

slow and turbulent blood flow in valve cusps aid in the development of thrombi. Local
tissue destruction also is an important reason for proximal thrombosis, and surgical
techniques may affect the risk of thrombus.
The clotting cascade is a self-regulating process that ends in the formation of a fibrin
thrombus. Two specific pathways are described: extrinsic and intrinsic. The extrinsic
pathway results from mechanical injuries (ie, trauma/surgery). Vein distension and
kinking, endothelial hypoxia, and vibration intraoperatively contribute to endothelial
damage. The intrinsic pathway involves circulating plasma factors. Both pathways meet
at the level of factor X, transformed into factor Xa. Three anticlotting mechanisms
prevent the formation of thrombi: antithrombin III, C and S proteins, and extrinsic
pathway inhibition (tissue factor). Intraoperatively, a reduction in circulating
antithrombin III prompts the clotting cascade. This reduction in antithrombin III is larger
and remains for a longer time after TJA than after non-orthopaedic surgical procedures.
Other factors may add to the particularly high risk observed in patients undergoing TJA.
These include injury to the deep veins from extremity positioning and femoral vein
compression as a result of flexion and adduction of the hip during hip surgery, the
anatomic position of the extremity and the use of a thigh tourniquet during knee
surgery, and bilateral rather than unilateral arthroplasty.
Risk Factors for VTE
Overview
Total hip and knee arthroplasty are considered high-risk procedures for VTE.
Specific groups of patients have an increased risk for VTE.

Overview
Many factors contribute to VTE. Recognized risk factors for VTE unrelated to surgery
include history of VTE, hypercoagulable states, thrombophilia, age, obesity, varicose
veins, family history of VTE, combined oral contraceptives, hormone replacement

therapy, anti-estrogens, pregnancy, puerperium, immobility, immobility during travel,
and central venous catheters.11 Total hip and knee arthroplasty are considered strong
risk factors for VTE for the aforementioned reasons. This in combination with the fact
that patients undergoing TJA tend to be older and typically have comorbid medical
conditions increases the risk of VTE.
Assessing the Risk of VTE
Risk factors for VTE can be divided into surgical and patient-related factors (Resource 1).
Surgical factors include the extent and duration of procedure, the type of anesthesia, and the
likelihood of postoperative immobilization.
Patient-related factors specific to arthroplasty include older age, poor ambulation, obesity,
cardiovascular disease, hypercoagulable states, and thrombophilia.

Assessing the Risk of VTE
The risk of VTE involves surgical and patient-related factors. Surgical factors include the
extent and duration of surgery (increased duration associated with increased risk), the
type of anesthesia (general anesthesia associated with increased risk compared with
neuraxial anesthesia), and the likelihood of postoperative immobilization. Many patient-
related factors can contribute to the risk of VTE, including previous VTE, cardiovascular
disease, Charlson comorbidity index score of 3,3 body mass index greater than 25 kg/m2,
family history of VTE, older age, and varicose veins. Among these, factors specific to
patients undergoing total hip and knee arthroplasty that are associated with an
increased risk of VTE include age older than 75 years (particularly older than 85 years3),
poor preoperative ambulation, obesity, and cardiovascular disease.12 Recent genetic
findings further highlight the importance of a history of VTE with regard to subsequent
risk after TJA and emphasize the importance of inquiring about previous VTE in obtaining
a patient’s preadmission history.13
In the era of personalized medicine and given the many existing pharmacologic options
for prophylaxis, researchers have focused on individualized risk scores; however, no

validated risk stratification algorithm exists for patients undergoing TJA. The Caprini risk
score is a risk assessment tool for the occurrence of VTE among patients undergoing
surgery; it includes 20 variables, and it is derived from a prospective study of 538
patients undergoing general surgery.14 Although the Caprini score can be used to
stratify the risk of VTE, the score was validated in patients undergoing non-orthopaedic
procedures.15 Therefore, investigators in several studies have tried to develop a score
more specific to TJA.16 Parvizi et al17 reported that knee surgery, Charlson comorbidity
index score, atrial fibrillation, previous DVT, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease,
anemia, depression, and body mass index were predictors for risk stratification. Bohl et
al18 reported that age, sex, body mass index, hematocrit level, and type of procedure
were helpful in risk stratification. Although these risk stratification protocols helped
identify patients at high risk of VTE, no recommendations regarding the optimal
prophylaxis regimen for these patients were identified. Results of various studies have
shown that different risk factors for VTE are critical, exemplifying the difficulty of creating
a risk stratification algorithm for all patients undergoing TJA. This approach has not yet
been incorporated into clinical practice. In addition, VTE may remain a substantial risk
despite adequate prophylaxis19 (Resource 2).
Assessing the Risk of Bleeding
It is important to evaluate the individual risk of major bleeding.
Risk factors for major bleeding include previous major bleeding, severe renal failure,
concomitant use of antiplatelet agent(s), history of or difficult-to-control surgical bleeding,
extensive surgical dissection, and revision surgery.

Assessing the Risk of Bleeding
Patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty are at high risk of bleeding (2% to
4%).20,21 Assessing the risk of major bleeding requires a complete patient history and
physical examination, including any previous major bleeding events, severe renal failure,
and simultaneous use of antiplatelet therapy. Surgical factors also must be considered
and include major surgical bleeding during current procedure, extensive dissection, and

major revision surgery. Patients at high risk based on history, patients with an underlying
bleeding tendency or thrombocytopenia (platelet count <50,000/μL), patients with
contraindications to pharmacologic prophylaxis (ie, active bleeding or intracranial
hemorrhage), and patients in whom the risk of bleeding is devastating (ie, Jehovah’s
Witnesses) should be considered for nonpharmacologic prophylaxis.
VTE Prophylaxis
Pharmacologic Prophylaxis
Overview
Numerous pharmacologic measures have been proposed for preventing VTE.
The optimal prophylaxis regimen remains unknown.
Aspirin has been gaining much attention in recent years and currently is used by more than
80% of TJA surgeons in the United States.

Overview
According to the American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) guidelines, various
chemoprophylactic agents can provide effective and safe VTE prophylaxis, including
unfractionated heparin (UFH), low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), adjusted-dose
vitamin K antagonists, factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban and apixaban), thrombin
inhibitors (dabigatran), and synthetic pentasaccharide factor Xa inhibitors
(fondaparinux). Based on their demonstrated efficacy, warfarin and LMWH were the
agents most commonly used for prophylaxis. In recent years, aspirin has been
increasingly used; however, its efficacy has not been definitely established because of
lack of randomized trials.
Aspirin


Aspirin
Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is an extensively studied oral antithrombotic agent that
irreversibly inhibits the activity of cyclooxygenase in platelets. Aspirin is widely available
and inexpensive, with a high safety profile compared with that of other
chemoprophylactic agents. Aspirin also is a milder agent associated with a decreased
risk of bleeding and hematoma formation. Aspirin also is unlikely to result in persistent
wound drainage, which is associated with the use of LMWH and other more aggressive
agents.22
Given these advantages, a drastic shift toward the use of aspirin as the main modality for
VTE prophylaxis after TJA has occurred in recent years.23 Although controversy remains
regarding its use as a single prophylactic agent for VTE, in a 2016 poll of members of the
American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons, more than 80% said they use aspirin as
the main prophylactic agent in patients undergoing hip or knee arthroplasty.
The Pulmonary Embolism Prevention trial is one of the most notable studies to
investigate aspirin as a prophylactic measure after TJA.24 Investigators in this
international, prospective study confirmed aspirin’s efficacy in preventing VTE for hip
fractures; however, no difference in symptomatic VTE events was observed between
patients who underwent THA and received aspirin and the placebo group. Based on the
results of patients with a hip fracture, the ACCP guidelines considered aspirin an
effective and safe form of prophylaxis. The efficacy of aspirin has been confirmed in
national, state, and institutional databases. In addition, the mounting evidence
supporting the safety and efficacy of aspirin after TJA resulted in the American Academy
of Orthopaedic Surgeons accepting aspirin as prophylaxis in patients undergoing
TJA;12,25,26 however, multicenter randomized trials are necessary to compare aspirin
with other more potent anticoagulants.
The optimal dose for aspirin has not been defined. The dose most commonly used has
been 325 mg twice daily; however, recent research has demonstrated that a low dose
(81 mg twice daily) is as effective.27 Studies also have shown that low-dose aspirin is
associated with a decreased incidence of gastrointestinal bleeding than higher doses.

Variation in aspirin sensitivity among patients remains an unresolved issue in relation to
the dose, and no routine screening test predicts this sensitivity.
Vitamin K Antagonists

Vitamin K Antagonists
This group of oral anticoagulants interfere with the cyclic interconversion of vitamin K
and its 2,3 epoxide, therefore controlling the γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues on
the N-terminal regions of vitamin K–dependent proteins. The advantages of warfarin are
that it has a long record of providing effective and safe prophylaxis after TJA and is an
oral agent. The disadvantages are that the international normalized ratio (INR) must be
monitored and that warfarin interacts with various drugs and foods that may influence
its biologic activity. Repeated blood testing is necessary for INR monitoring. The target
INR for patients undergoing TJA is 2.0. If warfarin is administered, an initial effect on INR
usually occurs within the first 2 to 3 days postoperatively. In a randomized trial, Colwell
et al28 compared the efficacy of warfarin with that of LMWH in patients undergoing TJA,
reporting no difference in the symptomatic events between the two agents; however,
the patients who received LMWH had higher rates of bleeding.
Unfractionated Heparin

Unfractionated Heparin
UFH is a combination of glycosaminoglycans that bind to antithrombin via a sequence of
pentasaccharides and catalyze the inactivation of various clotting enzymes. Heparin
cannot be absorbed through the gastrointestinal system; therefore, it is administered
intravenously or subcutaneously. The use of UFH may lead to hemorrhagic
complications. Because the response differs among patients, patients being treated with
UFH must be monitored (activated partial thromboplastin time) and doses adjusted
respectively. An advantage of UFH is that its anticoagulant effects may be reversed

rapidly with the use of intravenously administered protamine sulfate. Heparin-induced
thrombocytopenia (HIT) is the most important nonhemorrhagic adverse effect of UFH.
HIT is associated with the formation of anti-heparin antibodies/platelet factor;
thrombocytopenia; and prothrombotic effect that may contribute to hemorrhage,
thrombosis, and embolism and lead to death. UFH is infrequently used as a prophylactic
agent.
Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin

Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin
LMWH is a factor X inhibitor. In numerous randomized trials, LMWH was an effective
form of VTE prophylaxis in patients undergoing TJA. LMWH is administered via a
subcutaneous injection. The North American dosing regimen for enoxaparin is 30 mg
twice daily, and patients receive a 40-mg dose daily after discharge from the hospital.
The ACCP guidelines suggest that LMWH be considered the prophylaxis regimen of
choice because of its efficacy and safety demonstrated in randomized trials.
Postoperative bleeding is the major concern associated with the use of LMWH, which has
limited the use of LMWH among arthroplasty surgeons in the United States. These
agents usually are administered the day after surgery. LMWH is derived from UFH;
however, LMWH is considered safer and more efficient and predictable. LMWH has a
longer half-life and a lower risk of non-hemorrhagic adverse effects than UFH. Another
advantage of LMWH over UFH is that it does not require patients to be monitored. These
clear advantages explain why LMWH has replaced UFH almost exclusively as the means
of prophylaxis after TJA. Although uncommon, HIT remains a potential complication of
LMWH.
Fondaparinux

Fondaparinux

Fondaparinux is a synthetic agent and is administered via deep subcutaneous injection.
Fondaparinux is an indirect factor Xa inhibitor, and it has a specific anti-Xa activity
superior to that of LMWH and a half-life of 17 hours compared with 4 hours for
LMWH. Another advantage of fondaparinux is that it does not inactivate factor IIa and
platelets and HIT is not a concern.
Factor Xa and Direct Thrombin Inhibitors

Factor Xa and Direct Thrombin Inhibitors
The major advantage of newer oral anticoagulant medications is that they are oral
agents and do not require patients to be monitored. Rivaroxaban and apixaban are
direct inhibitors of activated factor X (factor Xa). Dabigatran is a selective and reversible
direct thrombin inhibitor. Results from well-performed multicenter, randomized
controlled trials have shown that rivaroxaban, apixaban, and dabigatran all reduced the
rates of VTE and all-cause mortality without an increase in the risk of major bleeding in
patients undergoing TJA; these patients received extended thromboprophylaxis for 35
days compared with conventional prophylaxis of 10 to 14 days.29 In most of these trials,
the drugs were administered 6 to 8 hours postoperatively; however, these drugs usually
are administered 18 to 24 hours postoperatively because of bleeding concerns.
Mechanical Prophylaxis
Overview
Mechanical devices should be used for prophylaxis in patients at high risk of bleeding.
Many surgeons use these devices in combination with chemical prophylaxis; however, data
supporting this practice are limited.

Overview

Mechanical prophylaxis methods should be strongly considered in patients with
contraindications to pharmacologic prophylaxis (eg, active bleeding, intracranial
hemorrhage, bleeding diathesis) and patients at high risk of bleeding (eg, coagulopathy).
This approach is based on study results suggesting that mechanical devices decrease the
risk of asymptomatic DVT by more than 50% compared with a placebo; however,
mechanical methods typically are less effective than chemical prophylaxis. Options for
mechanical methods of thromboprophylaxis include mobilization, intermittent
pneumatic compression devices (IPCDs), graduated compression stockings (GCS), and
venous foot pumps.
Mobilization

Mobilization
With improvements in pain control and the application of accelerated recovery
protocols, early walking has become easy to implement and has been linked to a lower
incidence of VTE after TJA.30,31 Although early walking is encouraged for many reasons,
most early VTE events occur after patients have started to walk. Therefore, mobilization
by itself is an inadequate means of VTE prophylaxis and should be used in combination
with other modalities.
Intermittent Pneumatic Compression Devices

Intermittent Pneumatic Compression Devices
IPCDs reduce plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 levels, stimulating endogenous
fibrinolytic activity, and are used in combination with anticoagulants to enhance their
effect. An IPCD usually is the preferred method of mechanical prophylaxis because most
of the data available on VTE after TJA are based on these devices. Interest also exists in

supporting the use of IPCDs for the prevention of VTE are limited and subject to bias.32
Graduated Compression Stockings

Graduated Compression Stockings
Data to support the use of GCS is mostly derived from fields outside of orthopaedic
surgery. GCS need to be sized and fitted properly and have been associated with local
skin breakdown. The hypothesis is that the GCS will reduce venous stasis and
thrombosis formation. Regardless, they frequently are used in combination with
pharmacologic methods in patients at high risk of VTE; however, it remains unclear
whether they are of any benefit to patients undergoing TJA.
Official Guidelines for VTE Prophylaxis
Overview

Overview
Organizations have made major efforts to provide strategies for VTE prevention. These
organizations include the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, the ACCP, and
the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. The ACCP guidelines have been
published for more than 20 years. The focus of the prior ACCP guideline in selecting
prophylactic agents placed more value on efficacy than safety and a great deal of
importance on the efficacy of a drug in preventing asymptomatic clots. This viewpoint
was of great concern to the orthopaedic community because surgeons were focused on
preventing symptomatic events and bleeding. The most recent guideline, which was
published in 2012 (9th edition), recognized the importance of symptomatic events and
bleeding in the selection of a prophylaxis agent.

American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons

American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
The most recent American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons guideline, published in
2011, did not recommend a specific prophylaxis regimen. The guideline was developed
based on network meta-analysis and was unable to recommend for or against any
specific VTE prophylactic agents because of lack of evidence. In addition, the guideline
did not delineate an appropriate duration of prophylaxis.
American College of Chest Physicians

American College of Chest Physicians
In 2012, the ACCP recommended that patients undergoing major orthopaedic surgery be
treated via one of the following prophylactic measures: LMWH, fondaparinux,
dabigatran, apixaban, rivaroxaban, low-dose UFH, adjusted-dose vitamin K antagonist, or
aspirin (all grade 1B). The use of LMWH was preferred over the use of other agents
(grade 2C/grade 2B). In patients receiving pharmacologic prophylaxis, the ACCP
suggested adding an IPCD during the hospital stay (grade 2C) and suggested extending
thromboprophylaxis for up to 35 days (grade 2B) postoperatively.
UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence

UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
In 2018, the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommended LMWH,
rivaroxaban, and aspirin as acceptable prophylactic agents for patients undergoing total
knee arthroplasty; however, after total hip arthroplasty, patients require 10 days of
LMWH before receiving aspirin or they may only receive oral Xa inhibitors or LMWH. This
recommendation was a major change compared with the previous UK National Institute
